newsitem.title: HUNGARY: Hungarian government outlines pension reform plans.
newsitem.headline: Hungarian government outlines pension reform plans.

text.p: The Hungarian government approved the guidelines of its pension reform plan, slated to go into effect in 1998, a government spokesman told a news conference on Sunday.
"The draft law package (of the pension reform) will be submitted to parliament on April 18," Elemer Kiss, Secretary of State of the Prime Minister's Office said following the government meeting.

Hungary needs pension reform that ties the amount of pensions paid out to social security contribution by individuals, and because demographic changes are likely to make the current system unfinanceable over the long term, the government said in a statement.
According to the guidelines, the current "pay-as-you-go" system, operated by the state social security funds will be completed with obligatory payments to private pension funds.

The new system will be obligatory for those who begin their carrier in 1998 or later, while those who will work for more than 15 years from next year can decide whether to join the new system, or stay in the old one.
Employees in the reformed system will have to pay six percent of their revenues as pension contribution to the private funds in 1998, seven percent in 1999, and eight percent from 2000.
They will receive some three-quarters of their pension from social security funds and the remainder from private funds.
Originally the government wanted the private funds to have a one-third share, but it decided against that during a wide public discussion of the guidelines, Kiss said.
He said the future rate of social contributions paid by employees to the social security funds would be decided when the government submits the social security's 1998 draft budget to parliament.
"But the calculations made so far show that the current rate could be reduced in the new pension system," he added.
Kiss said the social security system would be also modernized to improve the registration of contributions paid by each individual during the working years.
Hungary expects private pension funds to boost investments of domestic players in the country's fledgling capital markets.
As agreed with the International Monetary Fund in March 1996, Hungary undertook to pass the reform of the social security system in 1997. The system posted huge losses last year.
